_note: Milling of the staple grains into flour, which households eat, and bran, which animals eat. Each recipe takes one grain and the shaft work to grind and sift it; the grain itself is grown (wheat_kg, millet_kg, maize_kg). Maize is ground on a metate in practice; the shaft work and yield are the same order, so one recipe shape serves all three. Bran is a joint output with no reference price, a recorded waste (data/world/waste_heaps.json), fed to draught animals and herds (Complaints/544).

flour_kg.basis: per 1000 kg of sifted flour ground between stones from wheat, with the bran sifted out
flour_kg.yield_basis: MILLED AND SIFTED. Stones crack and grind the grain; the flour is bolted through a sieve and the husk and germ that stay on it are bran. Of 1190 kg of grain in, 1000 kg of flour (an extraction of about 84 percent, in the range of 75 to 85 percent usual for stone-milled bolted flour; recalled from milling handbooks, not opened, conf D), 150 kg of bran (about 12.6 percent, conf D) and 40 kg lost as moisture and dust (about 3.4 percent, the few percent the whole-meal entry this replaces took as its loss; conf C, author's estimate). Shaft work: grinding grain between stones takes on the order of a tenth of a megajoule per kilogram of grain (author's estimate from the output of a hand quern at the 75 W a person sustains, about a kilogram an hour, and of water mills; not checked against a primary source offline, conf C), scaled to the grain ground. The shaft work is priced through the energy market, so whoever supplies it (people at a quern or treadmill, or a water wheel and the millwrights who build and tend it) is paid there. Labour is feeding the hopper, dressing the stones, bolting and sacking, a few hours a tonne (conf D). Millstone wear is not charged. The bran carries no share of the cost (a recorded waste with no reference price); it is the winter supplement of herds and draught animals (95_herds.json, 94_agri_organics_gaps.json).
